source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify, Table 15 (prompt effects, paired permutation tests)
finding: Think-in-Opposites (TiO) raised task success for both groups of models. The rise was larger for thinking models. Dual-Goal helped thinking models and hurt non-thinking models. Only thinking models changed their I:C (share of tests that could falsify) significantly.
numbers: Thinking models: Dual-Goal +0.148 success, TiO +0.123 success (both p < 2e-5); I:C +0.375 (DG) and +0.168 (TiO), p < 2e-5. Non-thinking models: Dual-Goal -0.060 success (p = 0.0065), TiO +0.063 success (p = 0.0033); I:C change not significant (DG +0.048 p = 0.24; TiO +0.020 p = 0.60). 80 episodes per model per cell; 50,000 permutations.
limits: Corrects the earlier summary 'significant only for thinking models': the TiO success gain is small but significant for non-thinking models too; only the I:C shift is not. A non-thinking TiO gain with no I:C shift means the prompt helped by some route other than more falsifying tests.
agent_relevance: A contrast prompt is a cheap, small plus for non-thinking models and a larger one for thinking models. A Dual-Goal style prompt can hurt weaker models, so test it per model.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Failing to Falsify, Table 2 (tokens per turn) and appendix C.1
finding: The paper reports average tokens per turn with and without each prompt but runs no matched-budget comparison. For thinking models TiO raised tokens per turn by about 12% to 58%. Non-thinking and thinking modes also had very different caps.
numbers: Thinking mode tokens per turn, baseline to TiO (read from a garbled PDF table, verify before relying): Qwen3-8B 1088 to 1716 (+58%); Qwen3-32B 1030 to 1450 (+41%); Qwen3-14B 1179 to 1332 (+13%); R1-distill-Llama-70B 958 to 1073 (+12%). Non-thinking TiO tokens per turn were about equal to baseline (8.4 vs 8.4 for Qwen3-8B). Caps: non-thinking 256 new tokens per turn, thinking 16K; thinking traces stripped from history. Temperature 0.6.
limits: Success columns are also misaligned in the text extraction, so per-model success deltas are not safely readable; only the Table 15 averages (d01) are clean. Whether the 14B and 70B models gained while using only about 12% more tokens is suggested by the layout but not confirmed.
agent_relevance: Part of the TiO gain for thinking models may be extra thinking tokens. Gap 2 stays open: our harness must give the plain arm the same token budget (a longer plain prompt or extra sampled attempts) to find out.

source: Banatt et al. (2024) WILT, section 4.3 function-inversion experiment (re-read)
finding: Models were given test cases written by another model (reasoning stripped) and had to guess the rule in one turn. Pairing one model's test cases with another model's rule guessing often beat using one model for both jobs. o1-mini did worse with its own tests than with chatgpt-4o-latest's tests.
numbers: o1-mini with chatgpt-4o-latest's tests: 19 of 50 rules. Best single-model full run (Claude 3.5 Sonnet): 14 of 50. o1-mini full run: 13 of 50. The own-tests number for o1-mini is only in Figure 3 (a matrix), not in the text.
quote: composing the test case generation of one model and the function inversion of another model very often outperforms using a single strong model
limits: The own-model-both-roles control exists only as a figure cell. The 'own tests' run is single-turn and has no reasoning attached, so it is not the same as the full multi-turn run. The paper says WILT removes 'many of the advantages of a model that has scaled up inference-time compute'. 50 rules only.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that test quality is a separable skill and that tests from a different (or stronger) model help. It does not show that a split on ONE model helps. Gap 3 is partly answered: the gain looks like a stronger-tester effect, not a role-split effect.

source: Banatt et al. (2024) WILT, Table 1 (accuracy, repeats)
finding: Weak models repeat tests they already used, often with the same stated reason. Strong models rarely repeat. Test repetition tracks poor scores.
numbers: Average repeated tests per rule: GPT-4o 2.84, GPT-4o-mini 9.78, Llama 3.1 8B 6.68, Gemma 2 9B 7.72, Claude 3 Haiku 8.00, o1-preview 0.06, chatgpt-4o-latest 0.06. Accuracy: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 14/50, o1-mini 13/50, o1-preview 12/50, GPT-4o 9/50, GPT-4o-mini 6/50.
limits: Repetition is a symptom, not a cause: high-repeat models are also weak at other things.
agent_relevance: A code check that blocks an exact repeat of a past test is free. It does not test whether wording-only hypothesis revisions happen (gap 5).

source: Chari and Pattanaik (2026) Wild Guesses and Mild Guesses in Active Concept Learning
finding: In a number game with Gemini 2.5 Flash proposing Python rules, choosing queries by approximate expected information gain (EIG) over the LLM-generated hypothesis set was no better than random on easy rules and worse than the positive test strategy. It was better on rules where falsification mattered. All methods failed on hard rules.
numbers: Queries to converge (cap 50; DNF = did not finish), EIG / positive-test / random: square numbers 3/2/2; odd numbers 7/4/2; powers of 2 5/2/2; even numbers under 30 17/31/17; multiples of 3 or 7 8/DNF/13; numbers ending in 6 14/35/21; digits sum under 8 43/DNF/DNF; remainder 5 mod 9 31/DNF/41; one less than a prime DNF everywhere. 13 rules, one run each as far as the table shows.
quote: query selection cannot compensate for a proposal distribution that assigns negligible mass to the target concept
limits: Workshop-style preprint, no seeds or error bars shown, one LLM, particle posterior with a code-simplicity prior. The failure is partly a particle-collapse artifact of this implementation (the 'support-mismatch trap').
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 4: when the same LLM makes the hypothesis set, EIG gains are not guaranteed. They appear where the first hypothesis is too narrow (falsification needed) and vanish where the generator cannot produce the right rule. Use EIG as a tie-break among valid candidates, not as the only rule, and refresh the hypothesis set.

source: Piriyakulkij, Acquaviva, Langenfeld, Tenenbaum, Ellis (2026) Induction and Inquiry via Probabilistic Reasoning over Language and Code
finding: An LLM proposes hypotheses (programs or language), code reweights them, and the next experiment is picked by information gain over the particles. It fits human behavior better than pure LLM or pure Bayes. In a shopping question task it asked more informative questions than a plain prompt and ReAct.
numbers: No clean numbers in the text; results are in figures (Fig. 8: information gain per question, 4 questions, GPT-4 as main LLM). They deliberately used non-reasoning LLMs.
limits: Mainly a model of human behavior, not a benchmark of agent success. Finite product set with exact updates in the shopping task. Figures only.
agent_relevance: Same recipe as Choudhury and Grand (K15). It shows the pattern works when the LLM generates the hypothesis set, but gives no matched-token comparison.

source: Branchini, Bianchi, Burro (2025) Thinking in opposites improves hypothesis testing performance in Wason's rule-discovery task, Memory & Cognition
finding: Re-read this session. The numbers in the earlier evidence (b22, b23) are confirmed. Thinking in opposites nearly doubled success. Listing seed properties alone did nothing. The gain came at the first announcement, with fewer triples tested, not more.
numbers: N = 180 (88 male, 92 female), mean age 30.11 (SD 13.57), recruited from psychology classes, 60 per condition, random assignment. Success: opposites 78.33%, properties-only 38.33%, control 36.66%. chi2(2, N = 180) = 27.986, p < .001. Triples before each attempt: control higher than both training groups, chi2(2) = 44.325, p < .001. Minimum f2 = 0.129. Kappa 0.87 for flexibility coding.
quote: Thinking in opposites nearly doubled the success rate
limits: Country not stated (authors and ethics board are Italian). No independent replication reported. The opposites arm has one extra training step, so some gain may be elaboration, not opposites. Training time not equalised. Only 3 attempts. Earlier Branchini 2023 pilot by the same group.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: the numbers are now confirmed, but replication is still missing: one group, one design. For an LLM agent, 'name the opposite of each property of your test, then test it' is the cheap operator to try.

source: Branchini et al. (2025), discussion of earlier 2-4-6 work (Rossi et al. 2001; Gale and Ball 2012; Gorman et al. 1984, 1987)
finding: The paper says Rossi et al. (2001) gave 2-4-6 as a counter-example of decreasing numbers and got nearly twice as many test triples before the first announcement, over four times as much negative feedback, and over 50% first-attempt solutions. It cites Gale and Ball (2012) at about 75% with the 2-4-6 / 6-4-2 contrast pair against about 20% (4-4-4) and about 34% (9-8-1) for other pairs. It calls the Gorman et al. results mixed.
numbers: Gale and Ball 2012: about 75%, 20%, 34% as quoted by Branchini. Rossi 2001: over 50% first-attempt solutions.
limits: Second-hand through Branchini, not read in the original. A search summary also says Tweney et al. (1980) dual-goal gave about 60% first announcements vs about 20% standard, and that the correct solution does not strictly require the disconfirmation strategy (unverified).
agent_relevance: Three lines (Rossi counterexample, Gale and Ball contrast pair, Branchini opposites) point the same way: showing the contrast case, not just the confirming case, raises 2-4-6 success. All are one task in human samples, the first two reported by a source other than Branchini's own group only in part.

source: Abe et al. (2026) Evaluation of Deontic Conditional Reasoning in Large Language Models: The Case of Wason's Selection Task (EACL short paper), Tables 2 and 3
finding: Zero-shot chain of thought (CoT, cap 6,000 tokens) was not uniformly helpful on deontic Wason problems. It helped llama-3.3-70b, olmo-2 and gemma3-4b, and hurt gemma3-12b and gemma3-27b. Reasoning models scored 98 to 100 percent without CoT prompts.
numbers: Deontic accuracy % (zero-shot / few-shot / CoT): gemma3-4b 17.5 / 21.2 / 38.8; gemma3-12b 58.8 / 78.7 / 43.8; gemma3-27b 77.5 / 76.2 / 62.5; llama-3.3-70b 62.5 / 78.7 / 83.8; olmo-2-32b 36.2 / 38.8 / 57.5; gpt-oss-120b 100.0 / 98.8 / n/a; qwen3-32b 98.8 / 100.0 / n/a. Cells look like 80 problems each (values are multiples of 1.25). Errors fit matching bias better than confirmation bias.
quote: these results do not provide evidence for confirmation bias
limits: Selection task, not rule discovery. The CoT arm got 6,000 output tokens, the zero-shot arm 10, so token budgets differ by design. Exact-match scoring. Open-weight models only. Direction depends on the model, there is no trend.
agent_relevance: CoT length is not a safe lever: it helps some models and hurts others on the same task. Choose per model, with a measured test. Gap 7 stays open for rule discovery.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Mind Your Step (by Step): Chain-of-Thought can Reduce Performance on Tasks where Thinking Makes Humans Worse
finding: Chain of thought (CoT) cut accuracy on tasks where verbal deliberation also hurts people: implicit statistical learning, face recognition, classification with exceptions. The drop was large for the strongest reasoning model tested.
numbers: Implicit statistical learning (artificial grammar): o1-preview was 36.3 points lower than GPT-4o on a subset; GPT-4o direct 87.5% vs CoT 64.4% (-23.1 points, p<0.0001); Claude 3 Opus 70.7 vs 62.7; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 65.9 vs 67.7 (no drop, p = 0.969). Exception-pattern task: CoT stagnates near 80%, the share that are not exceptions. GPT-4o took up to 331% more rounds to learn the labels with CoT.
limits: Not a rule-discovery game with self-chosen tests. Tasks were chosen because humans also get worse. Older models (2024).
agent_relevance: Some induction tasks get worse with more verbal reasoning. The agent should not assume longer thinking helps hypothesis work; compare a short and a long arm on its own tasks.

source: Jin, Zhang, Luo, Wang (2025) Evaluating the Inductive Abilities of LLMs: Why Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Sometimes Hurts More Than Helps (NeurIPS 2025), search snippet
finding: Per the abstract seen in search: on four game tasks with hidden rules (chess, Texas Hold'em, dice, blackjack) CoT can hurt induction, and reasoning models often do worse than non-reasoning ones. Three failure types are named: wrong sub-task split, wrong sub-task solving, wrong final summary. Structured interventions fixed some of it.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Snippet only. Bertolazzi cites this as Jin et al. (2026).
agent_relevance: Independent support that longer CoT is not monotone for induction. Open the paper before relying on any figure.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench, re-read: method and failure analysis
finding: Re-read this session. Player and oracle are the same model but separate calls. Confirmation bias (share of positive tests) strongly predicts failure after controlling for oracle error. Failed games also drift into hypotheses that are disjoint from or partly overlap the target. Extended thinking was not enough for the smallest reasoning models.
numbers: 100 games, 12 models, 20-turn cap. Bayesian mixed-effects logistic regression, n = 1,200: confirmation bias posterior mean -4.15 (OR 0.016); oracle error -0.12 (OR 0.885, interval spans zero). Success: GPT-5.2-Chat 75%, GPT-OSS-120B 68%, DeepSeek-V3.1 41%, GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%. Spearman -0.779 (success vs bias), -0.937 (bias vs conclusive-falsification rate). Conclusive falsification: GPT-OSS-20B 59.2%, Llama-4-Maverick 18.0%.
limits: Hypothesis-target relations were labelled by GPT-5-Mini, not humans. Retry used low reasoning effort. Still correlational: no prompt or code intervention is tested.
agent_relevance: Confirms the correlation behind S4 but again nobody forces falsifying tests. Gap 1 stays open. It also shows a way to label 'hypothesis moved toward the truth' per turn, a base for a gap 5 check.

source: Analysis of Error Sources in LLM-based Hypothesis Search for Few-Shot Rule Induction (2025)
finding: In hypothesis-search pipelines the bottleneck is producing the right hypothesis. Refinement fixes crashes but almost never fixes a wrong idea.
numbers: 100 list-function tasks x 11 trials (5,500 trials), GPT-4o. Mean test accuracy: human 0.521, hypothesis search 0.487, direct generation 0.359 (GPT-4o) and 0.322 (Codex). Generator correct 46.4%; summarizer correct 34.5% and drops about 26% of correct generator hypotheses; implementor 61.2% train / 62.0% test. Refinement rescued 4.3% of semantically wrong hypotheses. Up to 257 LLM calls per trial. 45.4% of programs that passed the single held-out example still failed the true rule.
limits: List functions, not Wason. The judge was an LLM. Table counts sum to 5,509, not 5,500.
agent_relevance: Supports a code check that a revision changes predictions (G2/S5): LLM-driven refine loops mostly repair syntax, not ideas. Does not directly measure rewording; gap 5 stays open.

source: Cost-Effective Agent Harnesses for ARC-AGI-1 (arXiv 2607.06764, 2026)
finding: On ARC grid tasks, separating exploration from synthesis and letting the synthesizer spawn new exploration when its current program fails raised accuracy with a non-thinking DeepSeek V3.2. The oracle is a program run against the training pairs.
numbers: ARC-AGI-1 public eval, 400 tasks. Accuracy and cost per task: one-shot 15.5%, $0.002; structured CoT 30.0%, $0.004; explorer-definer pipeline (5 explorers) 54.75% pass@1, 57.5% pass@2, $0.25; reflective orchestrator 67.25% pass@2, $0.62. Paired deltas: CoT to pipeline +27.5, pipeline to orchestrator +9.75 [6.5, 13.25]. Explorer count N is the dominant lever (N=1 never above 45.5%). Qwen3-235B on 99 tasks: baseline 17.2, CoT 28.3, pipeline 48.5, orchestrator 54.6; orchestrator lift +6.06, CI includes zero. 69% of tasks solved only by the orchestrator had a winning run that called explore_new_patterns.
limits: Compared at very unequal cost (125x and 310x the one-shot baseline), so gains are not token-matched. The CoT arm is a cheap baseline. Author preprint, not peer reviewed. Generation-bound by its own diagnostic.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: a programmatic-oracle task that is not a number triple. Independent exploration breadth beat refinement, and re-exploring after a failed program helped. There is no test here of falsifying probes on ARC.

source: Xiong (2026) Hypothesis generation and updating in large language models (number game)
finding: LLMs by default assume the examples are drawn from the target set, which makes them prefer narrower hypotheses. Thinking mode shifts them toward relying on the prior. Models pick correct hypotheses better when evaluating than when generating, and their rule-like guesses fail to generalize beyond the examples.
numbers: Abstract and introduction read only; no figures extracted.
quote: by default they show a strong-sampling assumption that creates an implicit Occam's razor, favoring narrower hypotheses
limits: Abstract and first page only. Positive-example number game, no test choice.
agent_relevance: Explains why first guesses are too narrow (the case where negative tests are needed). Also an evaluation-generation gap: judging a candidate rule is easier than inventing one, which fits a candidate list judged by the model.

source: Dobrowolska et al. (2026) Tiny Moves: Game-based Hypothesis Refinement
finding: Restricting hypothesis edits to a small grammar of local moves removed more injected errors and kept valid parts better than prompting baselines, which tend to overwrite large parts. Change size was measured at entity and text level.
numbers: Abstract and sampled sections read; the main tables were not extracted.
limits: Pathway biology; corrupted-hypothesis recovery, not rule discovery. Partial read.
agent_relevance: Shows that how much a hypothesis changed can be measured in code (entity-level vs text-level change). That is the measurement a G2/S5 'is this only a rewording' check needs.

source: Macmillan-Scott and Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and cognitive biases in large language models, Royal Society Open Science (arXiv 2402.09193)
finding: Opened the arXiv text. The Wason results are in a figure, so the press figure (GPT-4 90% vs GPT-3.5 and Bard 0%) was NOT confirmed from the paper text. Overall, most wrong LLM answers were not human-like errors, and the same model gave different answers to the same prompt.
numbers: Seven models, zero-shot, 12 tasks including Wason in standard and facilitated forms. GPT-4 overall: 69.2% correct with correct reasoning. The 90% to 0% Wason range comes from press summaries, not the paper text.
limits: Wason cell values only in a figure here. 2023-era models.
agent_relevance: The 90% vs 0% item stays unverified; keep it out of the schema case. The within-model inconsistency supports sampling several attempts (G4).

source: Ragni, Kola, Johnson-Laird (2018) selection-task meta-analysis; Kellen and Klauer critique; Ragni and Johnson-Laird (2020) reply
finding: From search snippets: selections in 99 experiments were more redundant than simulated independent selections; Kellen and Klauer dispute the model comparison and say the favored model is non-identifiable; the reply is in Computational Brain and Behavior.
numbers: 99 experiments (from snippet).
limits: Snippets only. The result is about which cards ONE person picks together, not about independence between separate attempts by an agent. No source found that links it to resampling.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: no useful transfer found. For G4, correlation between repeated LLM samples of the same prompt is a separate empirical question; measure it in our harness through the diversity of hypotheses.

source: Dasgupta et al. (2022/2024) content effects; Seals and Shalin (2023/2024) social content in LLM reasoning
finding: Search summaries only: realistic framing helps LLMs and humans (Dasgupta); social content helps LLMs but less than humans, and format interacts with content in a non-human way (Seals and Shalin). No paper found that tests re-expressing an abstract rule as a concrete one as an intervention. Abe (d09) adds that deontic rules beat descriptive ones for every model and prompt, by 5.0 to 41.2 points.
numbers: No new numbers beyond d09.
limits: Snippets only; earlier evidence lines (b15, b21) hold the numbers.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open. The conflict may come from rule type and model era; the safe move is a small A/B in our own harness.

source: Search for code-enforced falsification ablations in LLM agents (Baby-AIGS 2411.11910; DiscoPER 2607.01131; Sound Agentic Science Requires Adversarial Experiments 2604.22080)
finding: Searches for a study that compares a code-enforced falsification step against prompt-only falsification at equal tokens found none. The nearest systems include a falsification agent or gate but do not run that ablation (per search summaries).
numbers: None.
limits: Negative search result from summaries, not from reading each paper. Absence of evidence.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 is open and is a real experiment to run: arms = plain, prompt-only falsify, code-gated falsify, at matched tokens, thinking and non-thinking models.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: Testing Inductive Reasoning with Hypothesis Refinement (ICLR 2024)
finding: From the abstract seen in search: LMs propose good candidate rules but apply them poorly; refinement with a symbolic interpreter helps. A rule-versus-application gap is reported.
numbers: None read.
limits: Snippet only.
agent_relevance: Run proposed rules in code; do not let the model judge them alone.
